title: The Office
text:
The Office (US) ran for nine seasons, from 2005 to 2013, and followed the employees of the Dunder Mifflin paper company in Scranton, Pennsylvania. Because every line of the show has been transcribed, the whole series can be treated as text data: who says what, how often, and how the show changed over time.
In this project I use string functions and regular expressions to answer three questions about my favorite show:

Who carries the show, and what happened when Michael Scott left?
Were episodes rated higher when Michael was in them?
What do the stage directions in the scripts reveal about each character?

title: The Office
text:
The data


Code
# install.packages("schrute") 

library(tidyverse)
library(schrute)
library(knitr)

office <- schrute::theoffice


Each row is one line of dialogue. The columns I use are season, episode, episode_name, character (who says the line), text (the line itself), text_w_direction (the line with the script’s stage directions in square brackets, such as “[laughs]”), and imdb_rating (the episode’s IMDb rating). The data has 55,130 lines across 9 seasons.

Cleaning the character names
The transcripts were typed by fans, so character names contain typos. Michael alone is misspelled ten different ways (“Micheal,” “Michel,” “Micahel,” and so on), and some names have stray quotation marks, periods, or capital letters. I clean the names in three steps: str_trim() removes extra spaces, str_remove_all() with the regular expression [".] deletes quotation marks and periods, and str_to_title() fixes capitalization (“MIchael” becomes “Michael”). Then fct_recode() maps the remaining misspellings to the correct name. About 120 lines are spoken by several characters at once (such as “Jim and Pam”); I leave those as their own speaker.


Code
office <- office |>
  mutate(
    who = character |>
      str_trim() |>
      str_remove_all("[\".]") |>
      str_to_title(),
    who = fct_recode(
      who,
      "Michael" = "Micheal", "Michael" = "Michel", "Michael" = "Micahel",
      "Michael" = "Michae", "Michael" = "M Ichael", "Michael" = "Micael",
      "Michael" = "Michal", "Michael" = "Miichael", "Michael" = "Mihael",
      "Dwight" = "Dight",
      "Angela" = "Anglea",
      "Darryl" = "Daryl", "Darryl" = "Darrly", "Darryl" = "Darry",
      "Phyllis" = "Phylis", "Phyllis" = "Phyliss"
    )
  )

title: The Office
text:
1. Who carries the show?
To see how the dialogue is shared, I keep the five characters with the most lines and lump everyone else together with fct_lump_n(). Then I calculate each character’s share of the lines in every season.


Code
season_share <- office |>
  mutate(who_top = fct_lump_n(who, n = 5, other_level = "Everyone else")) |>
  count(season, who_top) |>
  complete(season, who_top, fill = list(n = 0)) |>    # seasons where a character has no lines get a 0
  group_by(season) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(who_top = fct_reorder2(who_top, season, share))   # legend order matches line ends

michael_s1_s6 <- season_share |>
  filter(who_top == "Michael", season <= 6) |>
  pull(share) |>
  range()

others_first <- season_share$share[season_share$who_top == "Everyone else" & season_share$season == 1]
others_last <- season_share$share[season_share$who_top == "Everyone else" & season_share$season == 9]




Code
character_colors <- c(
  "Michael" = "#D55E00",
  "Dwight" = "#E69F00",
  "Jim" = "#0072B2",
  "Pam" = "#CC79A7",
  "Andy" = "#009E73",
  "Everyone else" = "grey60"
)

ggplot(season_share, aes(x = season, y = share, color = who_top)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = character_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "After Michael left, no single character replaced him",
    subtitle = "Share of each season's lines spoken by the five biggest characters",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Share of that season's lines",
    color = "Character",
    caption = "Data: schrute R package (fan transcripts of The Office)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 1





Each line shows one character’s share of all lines spoken in a season. For the first six seasons Michael speaks between 26% and 33% of all lines, about twice as many as anyone else. His share falls in Season 7, the season he leaves, and drops to zero in Season 8 (he only returns for a couple of lines in the series finale).
Nobody takes over his role. Andy, who joins in Season 3, gets his biggest share in Season 8 and briefly becomes the top speaker, but he never comes close to Michael’s level. Dwight and Jim stay roughly where they were, and Pam’s share actually dips. Instead, the gray line shows the dialogue spreading across the ensemble: the share spoken by everyone outside the top five grows from 27% in Season 1 to 54% in Season 9. The later seasons of The Office are much more of an ensemble show.

title: The Office
text:
2. Were episodes better with Michael?
Next I calculate, for every episode, the share of its lines spoken by Michael and compare it with the episode’s IMDb rating. Two-part episodes appear as a single episode in this data.


Code
episodes <- office |>
  group_by(season, episode) |>
  summarize(
    episode_name = first(episode_name),
    imdb_rating = first(imdb_rating),
    michael_share = mean(who == "Michael"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(season, episode) |>
  mutate(
    order = row_number(),
    michael = if_else(michael_share > 0, "Yes", "No") |>
      fct_relevel("Yes")
  )

season_starts <- episodes |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarize(start = min(order))

top_episodes <- episodes |>
  slice_max(imdb_rating, n = 1)

rating_with <- mean(episodes$imdb_rating[episodes$michael == "Yes"])
rating_without <- mean(episodes$imdb_rating[episodes$michael == "No"])
n_without <- sum(episodes$michael == "No")

michael_episodes <- filter(episodes, michael_share > 0)
r_within <- cor(michael_episodes$michael_share, michael_episodes$imdb_rating)




Code
ggplot(episodes, aes(x = order, y = imdb_rating, color = michael)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    data = top_episodes,
    aes(x = order, y = imdb_rating, label = episode_name),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    vjust = -1, hjust = "inward", size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = season_starts$start,
    labels = str_c("S", season_starts$season)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(6.5, 10)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Yes" = "#D55E00", "No" = "grey55")) +
  labs(
    title = "Episodes without Michael were rated lower on IMDb",
    subtitle = "IMDb rating of every episode in the order it aired",
    x = "Episode (tick marks show where each season starts)",
    y = "IMDb rating (out of 10)",
    color = "Does Michael have lines in the episode?",
    caption = "Data: schrute R package (IMDb ratings)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2





Each dot is one episode, placed in the order it aired, with its height showing its IMDb rating. Orange dots are episodes where Michael has at least one line and gray dots are episodes where he has none. The gray dots cluster at the end of the series and sit visibly lower: episodes with Michael average 8.41 while the 49 episodes without him average 7.81. Most of the lowest-rated episodes of the show come from Season 8, the first season without him. The two highest-rated episodes (both 9.7) are labeled: “Goodbye, Michael,” his farewell, and the series finale, where he makes a brief return.
However, among the episodes Michael is in, how much he talks has essentially no relationship with the rating (correlation 0). Episodes where Michael dominates the dialogue are not rated higher, on average, than episodes where he has a smaller part. So the plot doesn’t show that “more Michael is better,” but it instead highlights that the show was rated lower after he left, which could also reflect the show getting older and losing other writers and cast members at the same time.

title: The Office
text:
3. What the stage directions reveal

That’s what she said
First, a quick check on the show’s most famous running joke. The regular expression that'?s what she said, with ignore_case = TRUE, matches the phrase with or without the apostrophe and in any capitalization.


Code
twss <- office |>
  filter(str_detect(text, regex("that'?s what she said", ignore_case = TRUE)))

twss_michael <- sum(twss$who == "Michael")

twss_peak <- twss |>
  count(season) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 1)


The phrase shows up in 33 lines across the whole series, and Michael says it 23 of those times (70%). It peaks in Season 4, with 9 uses.


Laughing, singing, sighing, whispering, crying
The text_w_direction column keeps the script’s stage directions, which describe how a line is delivered: “[laughs],” “[whispering],” “[to Jim].” To pull them out I use a lookbehind and a lookahead together:

(?<=\[) is a lookbehind that requires an opening bracket right before the match,
[^\]]+ matches any characters that are not a closing bracket,
(?=\]) is a lookahead that requires a closing bracket right after the match.

The result is the text inside each pair of brackets, without the brackets themselves. Then I use five regular expressions to flag the kind of direction. For example, laugh|chuckl|giggl catches “laughs,” “chuckling,” and “giggles,” and \bsing(s|ing)?\b|\bsang\b catches forms of “sing” without matching words like “singular.” For each of the eight characters with the most lines, the table shows how many of their lines carry each kind of direction, per 1,000 lines, so that characters with more lines aren’t automatically ranked higher.


Code
directions <- office |>
  mutate(
    stage = str_extract_all(text_w_direction, "(?<=\\[)[^\\]]+(?=\\])"),   # text inside [ ]
    stage = map_chr(stage, ~ str_to_lower(str_flatten(.x, " | ")))         # one string per line
  )

summarize_directions <- function(df) {
  df |>
    summarize(
      lines = n(),
      laughing = 1000 * mean(str_detect(stage, "laugh|chuckl|giggl")),
      singing = 1000 * mean(str_detect(stage, "\\bsing(s|ing)?\\b|\\bsang\\b")),
      sighing = 1000 * mean(str_detect(stage, "\\bsigh")),
      whispering = 1000 * mean(str_detect(stage, "\\bwhisper")),
      crying = 1000 * mean(str_detect(stage, "\\b(cry|cries|crying|cried|sobs?|sobbing|tearing up|teary)\\b"))
    )
}

top8 <- office |>
  count(who, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  pull(who) |>
  as.character()

by_character <- directions |>
  filter(who %in% top8) |>
  mutate(who = fct_infreq(as.character(who))) |>   # most lines first
  group_by(who) |>
  summarize_directions() |>
  mutate(who = as.character(who))

direction_table <- bind_rows(
  by_character,
  directions |> summarize_directions() |> mutate(who = "All characters")
)

pct_with_direction <- mean(directions$stage != "")
andy <- filter(direction_table, who == "Andy")
everyone <- filter(direction_table, who == "All characters")




Code
direction_table |>
  select(who, lines, laughing, singing, sighing, whispering, crying) |>
  kable(
    digits = 1,
    format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
    col.names = c("Character", "Lines", "Laughing", "Singing", "Sighing", "Whispering", "Crying"),
    caption = "Stage directions per 1,000 lines for the eight characters with the most lines"
  )

Only 17% of lines carry any stage direction, so these rates are small, but a few characters stand out clearly. Andy has a singing direction 13.6 times per 1,000 lines, compared with 3.7 for the cast as a whole. That matches his character, a former member of Cornell’s a cappella group who breaks into song constantly. Erin has the most laughing directions, Angela has by far the most crying directions, and Michael leads the table in sighing. This makes sense with the character’s personalities in ways fans can note easily, such as Dwight having the highest whispering rate as the paranoid one of the bunch.

title: The Office
text:
What the text tells us
The first two sections tell one story from two angles. Michael speaks about a third of the lines for most of the show, and when he leaves the dialogue spreads out across the ensemble rather than shifting to a new lead. Over the same stretch the episodes’ IMDb ratings fall, even though, while he was on the show, episodes with more Michael were not rated higher than episodes with less. The stage directions add character detail that plain dialogue can’t: Andy sings, Erin laughs, Angela cries, and Michael, the boss responsible for 70% of the show’s “that’s what she said” jokes, sighs.
However, as someone with vast experience in NLP, I can confirm that there are limits to what this text can show. The transcripts and their stage directions were typed by fans, so different episodes may have been transcribed with different levels of detail, and a regular expression can’t tell a sarcastic “[laughs]” from a real one. Likewise, the ratings comparison can’t separate Michael’s absence from everything else that changed in the last two seasons.

title: The Office
text:
Data source
The data comes from the schrute R package by Brad Lindblad, available on CRAN (https://cran.r-project.org/package=schrute) and GitHub (https://github.com/bradlindblad/schrute). The package contains the full transcript of The Office (US) in tidy format, one row per line.
According to the package documentation, the original source of the transcripts is the fan transcription site Forever Dreaming (https://transcripts.foreverdreaming.org). The episode ratings and vote counts in the package come from IMDb.

title: Coffee Ratings
text:
This analysis uses the TidyTuesday dataset from July 7, 2020. It contains reviews of coffee beans by trained graders at the Coffee Quality Institute. Each row is one rated batch of beans. Along with the bean’s origin, species, and processing method, the data records scores for attributes like aroma, flavor, and acidity. Those scores add up to a total “cup points” rating out of 100.
The plot below compares total cup points across countries of origin. I only included countries with at least 25 rated batches, so that each box is based on a reasonable number of ratings. I also removed one batch with a recorded score of 0.


Code
library(tidyverse)

coffee_ratings <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-07-07/coffee_ratings.csv')

title: Palm Trees
text:
This analysis uses the TidyTuesday dataset from March 18, 2025, which comes from PalmTraits 1.0, a global database of functional traits for palm species (family Arecaceae). Each row is one palm species. The columns describe its growth form, stem and leaf measurements, and fruit characteristics.
Palms come in very different sizes. Some have no visible stem at all, and others grow into tall canopy trees. The plot below compares the maximum recorded stem height of each species across the palm subfamilies. Because heights range from well under a meter to tens of meters, the x-axis uses a log scale.

library(tidyverse)

palmtrees <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-18/palmtrees.csv')

title: The Office Writers
text: One of my favorite fun facts is that several of the people who wrote episodes of The Office were also in the cast! In this project I test whether the episodes they wrote were rated higher on IMDb than episodes written by everyone else, by more than we would expect if the writer had nothing to do with the rating. I write a function that randomly shuffles which episodes count as “actor-writer” episodes and recomputes the gap in mean rating, and then I use map_dbl() to repeat that shuffle 5,000 times to see what gaps chance alone produces. Because the actor-writers wrote most of their episodes in the early seasons, which were rated higher on average than the later ones, I also run a second version of the test that only shuffles episodes within the same season.

title: The Office Writers
text:
Background and research question
The Office (US) ran for nine seasons on NBC, from 2005 to 2013. Several of its writers were also in the cast:

Mindy Kaling, who played Kelly Kapoor (this is my favorite character!)
B.J. Novak, who played Ryan Howard
Paul Lieberstein, who played Toby Flenderson
Michael Schur, who played Mose Schrute, Dwight’s cousin
Steve Carell, who played Michael Scott

For the sake fo this project, I call these five the actor-writers. Additionally, I only count writers who played a main or recurring character, not writers who showed up once as a guest.
This question came to my mind because an actor-writer knows the characters from the inside. They perform in the scenes, they know what the other actors do well, and they have a personal stake in how the show turns out. I believe that if that inside knowledge makes for better episodes, their episodes should be rated higher. However, every script on a show like this gets rewritten by the whole writers’ room, so the name in the credits might not matter at all.
This is my research question: Do episodes of The Office written by an actor-writer have a higher mean IMDb rating than episodes written by other writers?
The variables I use are:

imdb_rating: the episode’s average rating on IMDb, out of 10, based on roughly 1,400 to 7,900 user votes per episode
writer: the episode’s credited writers (co-written episodes list several names separated by semicolons)
actor_writer: a variable I create, TRUE if at least one credited writer is an actor-writer and FALSE otherwise
season: the season the episode aired in, which I use in the second version of the test

title: The Office Writers
text:
The data


Code
# install.packages("schrute")

library(tidyverse)
library(schrute)
library(knitr)

office <- schrute::theoffice




Code
actor_writers <- c("Mindy Kaling", "B.J. Novak", "Paul Lieberstein",
                   "Michael Schur", "Steve Carell")

# theoffice has one row per line of dialogue, so we collapse it to one row per episode
episodes <- office |>
  mutate(season = as.integer(season), episode = as.integer(episode)) |>
  group_by(season, episode) |>
  summarize(
    episode_name = first(episode_name),
    writer = first(writer),
    imdb_rating = first(imdb_rating),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # we split each credit into names, then check each episode for an actor-writer
    actor_writer = map_lgl(
      str_split(writer, ";"),
      \(people) any(str_trim(people) %in% actor_writers)
    ),
    writer_type = if_else(actor_writer, "Actor-writer", "Other writers")
  )

aw_by_season <- episodes |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarize(aw = sum(actor_writer), total = n())

# single numbers are used in the text
n_aw <- episodes |> filter(actor_writer) |> nrow()
n_other <- episodes |> filter(!actor_writer) |> nrow()
s2_aw <- aw_by_season |> filter(season == 2) |> pull(aw)
s2_total <- aw_by_season |> filter(season == 2) |> pull(total)
s9_aw <- aw_by_season |> filter(season == 9) |> pull(aw)
s9_total <- aw_by_season |> filter(season == 9) |> pull(total)


Each row of theoffice is one line of dialogue, so I first collapse the data to one row per episode. It is important to note that two-part episodes, which are some of the most popular, appear as a single episode in this data, which leaves 186 episodes. Of these, 63 were written or co-written by an actor-writer and the other 123 were written by other writers. To flag the actor-writer episodes, str_split() breaks each writing credit into separate names, and map_lgl() goes through the episodes one at a time and checks whether any of those names is on the actor-writer list. I match full names exactly, so a different writer with the same last name, Warren Lieberstein, is not counted.
Data source: I got the data from the schrute R package by Brad Lindblad (https://bradlindblad.github.io/schrute/), installed from CRAN. The idea for the use of this dataset came from TidyTuesday, as the same data was featured in TidyTuesday on March 17, 2020 (https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2020/2020-03-17). As for where the information originally comes from: the transcripts were typed up by fans on the Forever Dreaming transcripts site (https://transcripts.foreverdreaming.org), which the package author scraped. The writer credits come from a table of each episode’s credited writers and directors that the package author added, and the IMDb ratings are averages of votes by IMDb users, which TidyTuesday collected from data.world in 2020 and the package joined onto the transcripts.

A first look at the original data

group_summary <- episodes |>
  group_by(writer_type) |>
  summarize(
    episodes = n(),
    mean_rating = mean(imdb_rating),
    median_rating = median(imdb_rating),
    sd_rating = sd(imdb_rating),
    lowest = min(imdb_rating),
    highest = max(imdb_rating)

# single numbers used in the text

Code
set.seed(47)

writer_colors <- c("Actor-writer" = "#D55E00", "Other writers" = "grey55")

ggplot(episodes, aes(x = writer_type, y = imdb_rating, color = writer_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5, color = "grey30") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 5, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = writer_colors) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Episodes written by actor-writers were rated higher on IMDb",
    subtitle = "Each dot is one episode; the black diamond marks each group's mean",
    x = "Who wrote the episode",
    y = "IMDb rating (out of 10)",
    caption = "Data: schrute R package (IMDb ratings and writing credits)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 1





The table gives summary statistics for each group, and the plot shows every episode behind them. Each dot is one episode, and the box shows the middle half of each group’s ratings. The black diamonds mark the group means: 8.46 for actor-writer episodes and 8.14 for episodes by other writers, a gap of 0.31 points. The whole actor-writer box sits a little higher, and the spread is narrower: their lowest-rated episode scores 7.5, while episodes by other writers go as low as 6.7. None of the ten lowest-rated episodes of the series were written by an actor-writer.
A gap of 0.31 might sound small, but most episodes of this show are rated between about 7.5 and 9 (we have to keep in mind that this is an extremely popular TV show), so it is a bit more than half of a standard deviation of the ratings (0.58 SD). The question for the simulation is whether a gap this big could easily happen by chance.

title: The Office Writers
text:
Is it just the seasons?
In my earlier page on The Office I found that the show was rated lower in its last seasons. That matters here, because the actor-writers did not write evenly across the show’s run.


Code
season_means <- episodes |>
  group_by(season, writer_type) |>
  summarize(mean_rating = mean(imdb_rating), n_episodes = n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(season_means, aes(x = season, y = mean_rating, color = writer_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_episodes)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = writer_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(1.5, 6)) +
  labs(
    title = "Actor-writers wrote fewer episodes in the later, lower-rated seasons",
    subtitle = "Mean IMDb rating of each season's episodes, split by type of writer",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Mean IMDb rating (out of 10)",
    color = "Episode written by",
    size = "Number of episodes",
    caption = "Data: schrute R package"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")








Figure 2





Each point is the mean rating of one group in one season, and bigger points mean more episodes. Two things stand out. First, the orange points get smaller over time: actor-writers wrote 13 of the 22 episodes in Season 2 but only 1 of the 23 in Season 9. Second, both lines are at their lowest in Seasons 8 and 9. So part of the overall gap could just be timing, as the actor-writers wrote more of the strong early seasons and fewer of the weaker late ones.
Nonetheless, the season-by-season comparison shows that timing is not the whole story. In the first four seasons the two groups are within 0.2 points of each other, but from Season 5 to Season 8 the actor-writer episodes are rated between about 0.1 and 0.5 points higher than other episodes from the same season (Season 9 has only one actor-writer episode, so that point says very little). To separate the writer from the timing, I run the test two ways.

Results


Code
ggplot(null_dist, aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "grey70", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff, color = "#D55E00",
             linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = obs_diff, y = Inf, label = "Real gap",
           color = "#D55E00", hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ shuffle, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "The real gap is bigger than almost every shuffled gap",
    subtitle = str_c("Gaps from ", scales::comma(reps),
                     " random shuffles of the actor-writer labels; the dashed line is the real gap (",
                     round(obs_diff, 2), ")"),
    x = "Difference in mean IMDb rating (actor-writer minus other writers)",
    y = "Number of shuffles",
    caption = "Data: schrute R package"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 3

  mutate(p_value = map_chr(p_value, format_p)) |>
  kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Type of shuffle", "Mean of shuffled gaps",
                  "Shuffles at least as big as the real gap", "p-value"),
    caption = str_c("Results of ", scales::comma(reps), " shuffles of each type")

Each histogram shows the 5,000 gaps from one kind of shuffle, and the dashed orange line marks the real gap of 0.31. The table lists, for each kind of shuffle, the average shuffled gap, how many shuffles produced a gap at least as big as the real one, and the resulting p-value.
The top panel shuffles the labels across all episodes. It is centered at 0, which is what we expect: when the labels are random, neither group has an advantage. The shuffled gaps almost all stay between -0.2 and 0.2, and none of the 5,000 were at least as large as the real gap, so the p-value is less than 0.0002.
The bottom panel shuffles only within each season, and it is centered at about 0.16 instead of 0. That is the gap we would expect from timing alone: because the actor-writers wrote more of the higher-rated early seasons, their episodes would average about 0.16 points higher even if, within each season, the label meant nothing. The real gap is about twice that size, and only 36 of the 5,000 within-season shuffles reached it, so the p-value is 0.0072.

title: The Office Writers
text:
Conclusion
Both p-values are well below 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis. Episodes of The Office written by an actor-writer have a higher mean IMDb rating than episodes written by other writers, and the gap is too large to be explained by chance alone, even after accounting for the season each episode aired in. About half of the raw gap of 0.31 points can be explained by timing, but the rest remains when episodes are only compared with other episodes from the same season.
It is important to be clear about what this result applies to. These 186 episodes are every episode of the show, not a random sample, so the test is not about some larger set of episodes. Instead, it asks whether the link between writer and rating is stronger than random assignment of writers to episodes would produce. The ratings themselves come from IMDb users who chose to rate the episodes, who are probably bigger fans than the average viewer, and the ratings are a snapshot from around 2020. So the conclusion describes how IMDb users rated The Office, not how all viewers felt about it, and it does not tell us anything about actor-writers on other shows.
The result also does not show that being in the cast made someone a better writer. The writers were not randomly assigned to episodes. Four of the five actor-writers had writing credits starting in the first season, so by the later seasons they were some of the most experienced writers on the show, and they may have been given the episodes that were expected to be big ones, such as the wedding episode “Niagara” or the Season 2 finale “Casino Night.” Experience or episode assignment could explain the gap just as well as acting experience.

title: The Office Writers
text:
What I did
I combined the dialogue-level schrute data into one row per episode and used str_split() with map_lgl() to flag the 63 episodes written by Mindy Kaling, B.J. Novak, Paul Lieberstein, Michael Schur, or Steve Carell. I wrote a function, perm_diff(), that shuffles the actor-writer labels and returns the new gap in mean IMDb rating, and I used map_dbl() to run it 5,000 times across all episodes and 5,000 times within seasons. The real gap of 0.31 points was larger than nearly every shuffled gap in both versions, so I concluded that actor-writer episodes were rated higher than chance would explain. Part of that gap is due to when the actor-writers wrote, and the rest could reflect experience or which episodes they were assigned, not only their acting.
